extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of logic, philosophy, and semantics (philosophers, logicians, linguists)
extracted.subtask_description: A taxonomy and pragmatic guidance for how names (words) should be understood and used in logic: distinctions between abstract/concrete, connotative/non-connotative, general/singular, positive/negative, relative, univocal/æquivocal/analogical, and how to fix connotation to promote clear thinking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract vs Concrete (use of 'abstract' in Logic)
rubrics_metrics.description: By 'abstract' (in Logic proper) mean the opposite of 'concrete'; an abstract name is the name of an attribute, a concrete name is the name of an object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author will always use 'abstract' to mean name of an attribute; resist the modern misappropriation of 'abstract' to mean 'general name'. Distinguish abstract names (names of qualities) from concrete names (names of things) when analyzing language and predication.

rubrics_metrics.name: General vs Singular Abstract Names
rubrics_metrics.description: Some abstract names are general (names of a class of attributes, e.g., 'color') while others designate a single attribute (e.g., 'visibleness', 'milk-whiteness') and so are not properly general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an abstract name designates only one attribute without variation in kind or degree, it should be considered neither general nor individual but placed in a separate class to avoid logomachy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principal-use criterion for a word's meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: A word ought to be considered the name of that which we intend to be understood by it when we put it to its principal use—i.e., when we employ it in predication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, 'white' in 'snow is white' is a name of subjects (things having the color), whereas 'whiteness' is the name of the color itself. Determine what a word names by examining how it is primarily used in predication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connotative vs Non-connotative (absolute) distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: A non-connotative term signifies a subject only or an attribute only; a connotative term denotes a subject and implies (connotes) an attribute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: proper names (John, London) and abstracts (whiteness, length) are non-connotative; adjectives like 'white', 'long', 'virtuous' are connotative because they denote subjects while implying attributes. Recognize connotation as central to meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: All concrete general names are connotative
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete general names (e.g., 'man') denote subjects (individuals) and connote the attributes those subjects possess (corporeity, rationality, human form).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that such names signify subjects directly and attributes indirectly; when defining or classifying, analyze the connotation (the attributes) that justifies the naming of the subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper names lack connotation
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper (individual) names denote individuals but do not imply or indicate attributes—they function as unmeaning marks attached to objects for identification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat proper names as carrying descriptive meaning; any information they bring is from prior associations, not from intrinsic connotation. Be cautious in logical analysis not to infer attributes from mere proper names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connotative individual names and individuation by context/qualification
rubrics_metrics.description: Some individual names can be connotative when their meaning includes an attribute unique to one individual (e.g., 'the only son of John Stiles'), or when a general name is individualized by context or modifiers (e.g., 'the present prime minister of England').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that definiteness (the article 'the', temporal modifiers, context) can turn a general term into an individual name in meaning. Analyze multi-word names and contextual limits to determine individuation and connotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning resides in connotation, not mere denotation
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever names convey information (have meaning), that meaning resides not in what they denote (the objects they name) but in what they connote (the attributes implied).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions of general names aim to declare or analyze connotation. To understand a name's meaning, identify the attributes it implies; listing all subjects to which a name applies does not by itself reveal the meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixing connotation to avoid vagueness and lax thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Names with indeterminate connotation lead to vague thinking; philosophers should aim, where practicable, to give every frequently used general concrete name a definite and fixed connotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When defining a general name already in use, strive to fix connotation with minimal change to the group's habitual application and minimal disturbance to commonly accepted truths. Exercise care since some vagueness may be pragmatically beneficial (e.g., classification in natural history).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indeterminate connotation vs multiple fixed connotations (ambiguity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish names with indeterminate (vague) connotation from ambiguous words that have several fixed, recognized senses (e.g., 'post', 'box').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambiguity properly treated is multiple distinct names sharing form; indeterminate connotation is conceptual vagueness that promotes sloppy thought. Scientific and philosophical writers must avoid using connotative terms without ascertained connotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive vs Negative names (and privative names)
rubrics_metrics.description: Positive names denote the presence of attributes (man, tree, good); negative names denote their absence (not-man, not-tree, not-good). Privative names denote the absence of an expected attribute while implying membership in a class that commonly has that attribute (e.g., 'blind').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a positive name is connotative, its negative counterpart connotes absence of that attribute. Note that form and reality may diverge: some words with negative form express positive attributes ('inconvenient' means causing annoyance). Analyze whether a term indicates mere absence or a positive peculiar attribute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative vs Non-relative (relative names imply correlates)
rubrics_metrics.description: Relative names (father/son, cause/effect, like/unlike) are always given in pairs and their signification implies existence of another correlated object; their attribute is a relation constituted by a series of facts involving multiple objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A name is relative when its meaning cannot be explained without mentioning another object. In analysis, identify the fundamentum relationis—the series of events/facts—that the relative names connote, and treat the two correlative names as different expressions of the same fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Univocal, Æquivocal, and Analogical (metaphorical) use of names
rubrics_metrics.description: A name is univocal when applied in the same sense to all things it predicates of; æquivocal when applied in different senses; analogical/metaphorical when secondary meanings derive from a primary meaning (e.g., 'brilliant' light vs 'brilliant' achievement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat æquivocal words as distinct names that happen to share form. Beware of fallacies that argue from a metaphorical use as if it were literal; analyze whether a usage is univocal, equivocal, or analogical to avoid ambiguity-based errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable vagueness in connotation must be guarded
rubrics_metrics.description: Some partial uncertainty in connotation can be harmless or even useful (e.g., in classification of natural history where looser grouping is practical), but it must be guarded by strict precautions to prevent lax habits of thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use looser connotation only where it serves practical ends; otherwise employ definitions or fixed connotations to preserve clarity. Philosophers should balance the difficulty of introducing new technical terms against the need to alleviate imperfections in everyday phraseology.
